summary: Remove all occurrences of val in place and return the count of remaining elements.
mainInsight: Copy every element that is not val forward to a write index; order of the kept elements is preserved and nothing is allocated.

approaches.name: Extra array
approaches.summary: Collect non-val elements and copy back.

approaches.name: Read/write pointers
approaches.summary: Write nums[j] to nums[i] when it is not val.

approaches.name: Swap with the end
approaches.summary: When nums[i] == val, replace it with the last element and shrink n.
strengths: Fewest writes when val is rare
approaches.interviewRelevance: Good variant when val is rare.

personalSolution.notes: Optimal; your comments also explain the extra-array brute force.

promptVariants: What technique removes elements in place with O(1) space?
Which two-pointer variant do you use for in-place filtering?
cards.explanation: A trailing write index records where the next kept element goes.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Converging pointers from both ends: That is the swap-with-end variant, less common.

promptVariants: What do nums[0..i-1] contain while the loop runs?
After processing nums[0..j], what is stored in nums[0..i-1]?
cards.answer: Exactly the elements seen so far that are not equal to val, in their original order; i is the next write position and the eventual answer.
cards.explanation: The tail beyond i is garbage and ignored by the judge.

promptVariants: Remove Element with read/write pointers is ___ time.
Extra space of the read/write approach: ___
Remove Element in place needs ___ auxiliary space.
When would swapping with the last element be better than read/write pointers?
Which Remove Element variant minimises writes when val is rare, and what does it sacrifice?
cards.answer: When val is rare: the swap version does at most one write per occurrence of val instead of copying every kept element, but it does not preserve the relative order of the remaining elements.
keyPoints: Fewer writes if val is rare
cards.explanation: Mention the trade-off when the interviewer allows reordering.

promptVariants: Why is it fine to overwrite nums[i] with nums[j] without saving nums[i] first?
What guarantees that overwriting nums[i] with nums[j] never destroys unread data?
cards.answer: Because i <= j always, nums[i] has already been read (it is at or behind the read pointer), so overwriting it cannot lose unread data.
cards.explanation: The same argument underlies most in-place compaction.
